MambaHybrid: Align-Mode State Management (torch reference)

This document translates MambaHybridModelState.preprocess_state and postprocess_state (vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/mamba_hybrid.py) into pure-torch reference implementations. The production versions launch fused Triton kernels (vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py) that do everything GPU-side with no CPU-GPU sync (async-scheduling safe); the torch versions below are semantically equivalent but sync (.item()), so they are for understanding / debugging / CPU fallback, not performance.

Overview

Mamba/hybrid models store recurrent state (conv windows + SSM temporal state) in KV-cache blocks: each (layer, state-type) state tensor is block-major, [num_blocks, ...], indexed through the request’s block table.

With speculative decoding (and chunked prefill), the “running state” — the state after the last accepted token — can land at a position that is not a multiple of the mamba block size (128 tokens by default). Align mode (cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align") handles this with three pieces per step:

  1. preprocess_state (before the forward): advance the running-state pointer to the block containing the last token of this step’s chunk, and pre-copy the state into the new block column when a boundary is crossed, so the forward kernels read the initial state from the write-side block.
  2. The forward: kernels write state in-place; num_accepted_tokens is passed via attention metadata as the in-block bias.
  3. postprocess_state (after sampling): record how many tokens were accepted, and if acceptance left the sequence non-block-aligned, save the running state at the block-aligned position (start of the next block).

Called from the model runner at:

  • vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1275 — preprocess_state, real batches only (dummy/profile runs skip it), before prepare_attn gathers num_accepted_tokens so the boundary reset is visible to the forward.
  • vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1204 — postprocess_state, right after post_update has advanced num_computed_tokens to the post-step count.

State layout & invariants

Per-request-slot GPU buffers (created in __init__, mamba_hybrid.py:75-95):

Buffer Meaning
state_idx[req] Block-table column holding the running state; -1 = fresh
num_accepted[req] In-block bias; 1 = neutral non-spec value
src_col[req] Pre-advance column (scratch, emitted by preprocess)
src_off[req] Accepted-token bias = num_accepted - 1 (scratch)

Seeded in add_request (mamba_hybrid.py:97-105): num_accepted = 1, state_idx = (num_computed_tokens - 1) // block_size (handles resumed / chunked-prefill requests).

State tensor layouts, per (layer, state-type):

  • Temporal (conv_width == 0): [num_blocks, state_len, ...] — copy whole block, token_bias selects the source column (bt[src_col + bias]).
  • Conv, SD layout: [num_blocks, state_len, dim] — contiguous window; copy shifts the window by bias: state[bt[src], bias:] -> state[bt[dst], :cw-bias].
  • Conv, DS layout (is_conv_state_dim_first()): [num_blocks, dim, state_len] — same shift, applied per dim row.

The block tables passed to these kernels are batch-order slices of the persistent input_block_tables (mamba_hybrid.py:149-156), so a row is indexed by batch position, while the decision arrays are indexed by req slot — the two are related by idx_mapping (with -1 sentinels for filtered rows under PP).

Shared copy primitive

Both methods funnel their copies through _copy_mamba_state_block (mamba_utils.py:27). Torch equivalent:

def _copy_mamba_state_block_torch(
    state: torch.Tensor,      # [num_blocks, ...] block-major state tensor
    conv_width: int,          # >0 = conv, 0 = temporal
    bt_row: torch.Tensor,     # [max_blocks] int32 block ids for one batch row
    src_col: int,
    dst_col: int,
    bias: int,                # accepted-token bias
    dim_rows: int = 0,        # DS conv: dim rows per block
    dim_first: bool = False,  # DS conv layout
) -> None:
    dst_block = int(bt_row[dst_col].item())
    if conv_width == 0:
        # Temporal: state[bt[src_col + bias]] -> state[bt[dst_col]]
        src_block = int(bt_row[src_col + bias].item())
        state[dst_block] = state[src_block]
    elif dim_first:
        # DS conv (num_blocks, dim, state_len): per-dim-row window shift
        src_block = int(bt_row[src_col].item())
        state[dst_block, :dim_rows, : conv_width - bias] = state[
            src_block, :dim_rows, bias:conv_width
        ]
    else:
        # SD conv (num_blocks, state_len, dim): contiguous window shift
        src_block = int(bt_row[src_col].item())
        state[dst_block, : conv_width - bias] = state[src_block, bias:conv_width]

Notes:

  • Empty slices (bias >= conv_width, or negative lengths) are silent no-ops, matching the kernel’s masked-to-nothing copy.
  • torch evaluates the RHS before assignment, so it is overlap-safe even if src_block == dst_block physically; the kernel does a raw memcpy there.
  • Block ids are used as advanced indices into dim 0; the kernel’s int64 widening (state strides can exceed 2³¹ bytes) is implicit in torch.

preprocess_state

Production (mamba_hybrid.py:160-207) launches two kernels: preprocess_mamba_align_fused_kernel (per-request advance + param emission) then ctx.run_fused_precopy (per (request, state) copies).

def preprocess_state_torch(
    state_tensors: list[torch.Tensor],   # per (layer, state-type), block-major
    conv_widths: list[int],
    group_indices: list[int],            # per state: which mamba group
    dim_row_counts: list[int],           # per state: dim rows (DS conv)
    block_tables: list[torch.Tensor],    # per group, BATCH order [num_reqs, max_blocks] int32
    idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,           # [num_reqs] int32: batch -> req slot
    num_computed: torch.Tensor,          # [max_num_reqs] int32: pre-step computed count
    query_start_loc: torch.Tensor,       # [num_reqs + 1] int32
    state_idx: torch.Tensor,             # [max_num_reqs] int32, in/out
    num_accepted: torch.Tensor,          # [max_num_reqs] int32, in/out
    src_col: torch.Tensor,               # [max_num_reqs] int32 scratch, out
    src_off: torch.Tensor,               # [max_num_reqs] int32 scratch, out
    block_size: int,
    dim_first: bool = False,
) -> None:
    num_reqs = idx_mapping.shape[0]
    mask = idx_mapping >= 0
    req = idx_mapping.clamp(min=0)

    # Stage 1: advance state_idx + emit pre-copy params
    # (preprocess_mamba_align_fused_kernel, mamba_utils.py:282)
    old_state_idx = state_idx[req].clone()
    old_num_accepted = num_accepted[req].clone()

    src_col[req] = torch.where(mask, old_state_idx, src_col[req])
    src_off[req] = torch.where(
        mask, (old_num_accepted - 1).clamp(min=0), src_off[req]
    )

    query_len = query_start_loc[1:] - query_start_loc[:-1]
    computed_after = num_computed[req] + query_len
    new_state_idx = (computed_after + block_size - 1) // block_size - 1
    state_idx[req] = torch.where(mask, new_state_idx, state_idx[req])

    # Reset the bias to neutral (1) when the running state crosses a block
    # boundary: after migration it sits at the start of the new block.
    crossed = mask & (old_state_idx >= 0) & (old_state_idx != new_state_idx)
    num_accepted[req] = torch.where(
        crossed, torch.ones_like(new_state_idx), old_num_accepted
    )

    # Stage 2: migrate state across boundaries
    # (precopy_mamba_align_fused_kernel, mamba_utils.py:329)
    for b in range(num_reqs):
        if not mask[b].item():
            continue
        r = int(req[b].item())
        s = int(src_col[r].item())
        d = int(state_idx[r].item())
        if s < 0 or s == d:
            # Fresh request, or still writing the same block: the forward
            # locates the initial state in-block via num_accepted.
            continue
        bias = int(src_off[r].item())
        for state, cw, gid, nrows in zip(
            state_tensors, conv_widths, group_indices, dim_row_counts
        ):
            _copy_mamba_state_block_torch(
                state, cw, block_tables[gid][b], s, d, bias, nrows, dim_first
            )

Semantics per request: computed_after is the post-chunk computed count (pre-step num_computed + this step’s query_len); the running state moves to column ceil(computed_after / block_size) - 1. The pre-copy migrates the state from the pre-advance column (src_col, with bias num_accepted - 1) to the new column, so the forward can initialize from the write-side block.

postprocess_state

Production (mamba_hybrid.py:289-328) scatters the accepted counts (_scatter_num_accepted_kernel, or index_fill_ for a scalar), then — in align mode with a post-step num_computed_tokens — runs run_fused_postprocess_align (postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel with PRECOMPUTED_NEW_COMPUTED=True, HAS_IDX_MAPPING=True).

def postprocess_state_torch(
    state_tensors: list[torch.Tensor],
    conv_widths: list[int],
    group_indices: list[int],
    dim_row_counts: list[int],
    block_tables: list[torch.Tensor],    # per group, BATCH order
    idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,           # [num_reqs] int32: batch -> req slot (-1 skip)
    num_sampled: torch.Tensor | int,     # [num_reqs] int32 or scalar
    num_computed: torch.Tensor,          # [max_num_reqs] int32: post-step computed count
    state_idx: torch.Tensor,             # [max_num_reqs] int32, in
    num_accepted: torch.Tensor,          # [max_num_reqs] int32, in/out
    block_size: int,
    dim_first: bool = False,
) -> None:
    num_reqs = idx_mapping.shape[0]
    mask = idx_mapping >= 0
    req = idx_mapping.clamp(min=0)

    # Stage 1: record accepted counts. Neutral value is 1: chunked-prefill
    # rows sample nothing (num_sampled == 0) but mamba treats 1 as non-spec.
    if isinstance(num_sampled, int):
        vals = torch.full(
            (num_reqs,), max(num_sampled, 1),
            dtype=torch.int32, device=idx_mapping.device,
        )
    else:
        vals = num_sampled.clamp(min=1)
    num_accepted[req] = torch.where(mask, vals, num_accepted[req])

    # Stage 2: save the running state at the block-aligned position when
    # acceptance left the sequence non-block-aligned
    # (postprocess_mamba_fused_kernel, mamba_utils.py:154)
    for b in range(num_reqs):
        if not mask[b].item():
            continue
        r = int(req[b].item())
        new_comp = int(num_computed[r].item())
        num_acc = int(num_accepted[r].item())
        src = int(state_idx[r].item())

        # Position (1-based) of the state currently saved in the running
        # block: the always-accepted sampled token of this step.
        running_pos = new_comp - num_acc + 1

        aligned = (new_comp // block_size) * block_size
        if aligned < running_pos:
            continue  # accepted progress stayed within the running block

        bias = aligned - running_pos
        dst = aligned // block_size - 1

        if src == dst:
            num_accepted[r] = 1  # state stays in the running block: neutral bias
        if src == dst and bias == 0:
            continue  # no-op self-copy

        for state, cw, gid, nrows in zip(
            state_tensors, conv_widths, group_indices, dim_row_counts
        ):
            _copy_mamba_state_block_torch(
                state, cw, block_tables[gid][b], src, dst, bias, nrows, dim_first
            )

Decision logic: running_pos is where the saved state currently sits (the sampled token is always accepted, regardless of draft rejections); new_comp is the post-step computed count = position of the last accepted token. If the accepted progress reaches a block boundary at or beyond the saved position (aligned >= running_pos), the running state is re-saved at that boundary: shifted forward by bias tokens into column aligned // block_size - 1 — i.e. the state at the start of the next block, which is what the next step’s preprocess/forward expects as its initial state. The num_accepted = 1 reset covers the same-block case: the state stays where it is and the in-block offset convention restarts at the block start.

Why GPU-resident?

The two production kernels run unconditionally each step and fast-exit per request (src_col < 0 or src_col == dst_col in preprocess; aligned < running_pos in postprocess). Skipping the launches would require an async D2H of the actual num_computed, since num_computed_tokens_np is an optimistic mirror under async scheduling — the launch cost is ~0.3% of TPOT, so the GPU fast-exit wins (mamba_hybrid.py:181-186).

Caveats of the torch reference

  • .item() calls sync GPU→CPU per request; use them for reference/testing only. A GPU-only variant would keep everything as tensors (the temporal copies vectorize to one advanced-index assignment; conv copies need per-bias bucketing because the slice length varies).
  • Block tables must be batch order (V2); the V1 kernel variant (HAS_IDX_MAPPING=False) uses req-slot order with req_idx = batch_idx.
  • The V1 postprocess variant (PRECOMPUTED_NEW_COMPUTED=False) derives the positions from pre-step values instead: running_pos = num_computed + num_scheduled - num_draft and new_comp = running_pos + num_accepted - 1, and writes the reset to a separate output buffer instead of in place.
  • Only align mode is covered here; the “all” mamba cache mode has its own lighter-weight bookkeeping (postprocess_mamba_all, mamba_utils.py:1140).

Model Runner V2: Code Walkthrough

This document explains the execution path of Model Runner V2 (MRV2), centered on vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py. It is intended as a code-reading guide. The higher-level design rationale is in model_runner_v2.md.

MRV2 is a per-worker orchestration layer. It does not implement transformer layers. Instead, it connects scheduler state, GPU-resident request state, attention/KV-cache metadata, CUDA graphs, the model, sampling, and output processing.

1. Code structure

flowchart TD
    S["SchedulerOutput"] --> R["GPUModelRunner.execute_model"]
    R --> U["Update request and KV state"]
    U --> I["prepare_inputs"]
    I --> A["prepare_attn"]
    A --> D["dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp"]
    D --> M["ModelState.prepare_inputs / prepare_attn"]
    M --> F["Model forward: eager, PIECEWISE, or FULL CUDA graph"]
    F --> X["ExecuteModelState"]
    X --> T["sample_tokens"]
    T --> L["Compute logits and sample"]
    L --> P["postprocess_sampled"]
    P --> G["Speculator proposal and KV connector"]
    G --> O["AsyncOutput / ModelRunnerOutput"]

    R -. "last PP rank" .-> T
    R -. "non-last PP rank" .-> PP["IntermediateTensors"]

    RS["RequestState"] --> I
    IB["InputBuffers / InputBatch"] --> I
    BT["BlockTables / KV cache"] --> A
    CG["ModelCudaGraphManager"] --> D
    MS["DefaultModelState or model-specific state"] --> M
    K["Triton input/update kernels"] --> I
    K --> P

The main state objects have deliberately different lifetimes:

Object Lifetime Responsibility
RequestState Persistent across steps Fixed slots for request IDs, token history, computed-token counters, draft tokens, and sequence limits.
InputBuffers Persistent buffers reused by steps GPU buffers for token IDs, positions, query offsets, and sequence lengths.
InputBatch One forward step The current request ordering, mappings, lengths, logits positions, and views into InputBuffers.
ModelState Persistent model-specific state RoPE, multimodal inputs, encoder-decoder state, Mamba state, and model-specific attention metadata.
ExecuteModelState Between forward and output processing Hidden states and metadata retained for sample_tokens() or pool().
BlockTables Persistent Maps logical request positions to paged KV-cache blocks and computes slot mappings.
ModelCudaGraphManager Persistent after KV initialization Captures and dispatches compatible CUDA graphs.

The runner is created by the worker when use_v2_model_runner is enabled; see gpu_worker.py around the MRV2 construction branch.

2. Lifecycle of one step

The public step is split into a forward phase and a result phase:

SchedulerOutput
      |
      v
execute_model()
      |-- request/KV state updates
      |-- input and attention metadata preparation
      |-- model forward
      `-- save ExecuteModelState
                |
                v
sample_tokens() or pool()
      |-- logits/sampling or pooling
      |-- update GPU request state
      |-- speculative draft proposal
      `-- asynchronous output copy

This split is important for asynchronous scheduling. The engine can enqueue a forward and then enqueue sampling without synchronously materializing the result on the host. See EngineCore.step_with_batch_queue() and AsyncOutput.

3. execute_model

GPUModelRunner.execute_model() coordinates everything needed to launch one model forward.

3.1 Update persistent request state

For a real batch, the runner first processes lifecycle changes:

self.update_pp_decode_requests()
self.finish_requests(scheduler_output)
self.free_states(scheduler_output)
self.add_requests(scheduler_output)
self.update_requests(scheduler_output)
self.block_tables.apply_staged_writes()

This is at model_runner.py:1217.

The operations include:

  • Removing finished and preempted requests.
  • Adding new or resumed requests into fixed RequestState slots.
  • Updating the CPU mirror of num_computed_tokens for cached requests.
  • Appending newly allocated KV-cache blocks.
  • Zeroing fresh cache blocks when required.
  • Applying copy-on-write KV-cache block copies.

New request data is staged before the forward. RequestState.apply_staged_writes() then commits token history, lengths, and the initial computed-token count to the GPU/UVA-visible state.

If there are no scheduled tokens, the runner skips the model and asks the KV connector for a no-forward result.

3.2 Select the execution shape

The runner derives:

num_reqs = len(scheduler_output.num_scheduled_tokens)
num_toks = scheduler_output.total_num_scheduled_tokens
max_query_len = max(scheduler_output.num_scheduled_tokens.values())
uniform_tok_count = get_uniform_token_count(
    num_reqs, num_toks, max_query_len
)

It also accounts for active LoRA adapters and forces eager execution for some dynamic encoder-decoder updates. Then it calls dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp().

The returned BatchExecutionDescriptor contains the selected:

  • CUDA graph mode: NONE, PIECEWISE, or FULL.
  • Padded token count.
  • Padded request count, when needed.
  • Uniform token count, when applicable.
  • Effective active-LoRA capture case.

3.3 Prepare the InputBatch

For real work, execute_model() calls:

input_batch = self.prepare_inputs(scheduler_output, batch_desc)
block_tables, slot_mappings = self.prepare_attn(input_batch)

These are described in the next sections. The important distinction is that RequestState stores persistent state in stable request slots, while InputBatch gathers those slots into the order required by this step.

3.4 Prepare model-specific and multimodal inputs

The first pipeline rank may run a multimodal encoder and produce inputs_embeds. Then the model-specific state contributes additional inputs:

model_inputs = {
    "input_ids": input_ids,
    "positions": input_batch.positions,
    "inputs_embeds": inputs_embeds,
    "intermediate_tensors": None,
    **self.model_state.prepare_inputs(input_batch, self.req_states),
}

For non-first pipeline ranks, token IDs and embeddings are removed and the received IntermediateTensors are copied into persistent buffers. This is needed because CUDA graphs require stable addresses.

3.5 Run the model

There are three execution paths:

if batch_desc.cg_mode == CUDAGraphMode.FULL:
    model_output = self.cudagraph_manager.run_fullgraph(batch_desc)
elif batch_desc.cg_mode == CUDAGraphMode.PIECEWISE:
    model_output = self.cudagraph_manager.run_pw_graph(
        self.model, model_inputs
    )
else:
    model_output = self.model(**model_inputs)

The actual code wraps the eager and piecewise paths in set_forward_context(), which publishes attention metadata, slot mappings, padding, DP token counts, and the runtime CUDA-graph mode to the model and attention layers. See model_runner.py:1385.

3.6 Save the forward result

The last pipeline rank receives hidden states. Earlier ranks receive IntermediateTensors. MRV2 saves the result in:

self.execute_model_state = ExecuteModelState(
    input_batch=input_batch,
    attn_metadata=attn_metadata,
    slot_mappings_by_layer=slot_mappings_by_layer,
    hidden_states=hidden_states,
    aux_hidden_states=aux_hidden_states,
    finished_req_ids=finished_req_ids,
)

See model_runner.py:1440.

  • Non-last pipeline ranks return IntermediateTensors immediately.
  • The last rank returns None; the caller then invokes sample_tokens().

4. prepare_inputs

prepare_inputs() converts the scheduler’s ragged per-request token counts into a contiguous GPU input layout.

4.1 Request ordering and slot mapping

MRV2 orders requests as decode, short extension, then prefill. It builds:

  • req_ids: request order for this step.
  • idx_mapping: batch row → persistent RequestState slot.
  • idx_mapping_np: host version used for bookkeeping.
  • expanded_idx_mapping: per-logit mapping used by speculative decoding.

The batch row does not have to equal the persistent request slot. This indirection is what allows requests to retain stable state while each step uses an execution-friendly order.

4.2 Query offsets and padding

query_start_loc is the cumulative sum of scheduled tokens:

query_start_loc = [0,
                   q0,
                   q0 + q1,
                   ...]

The host constructs a NumPy copy and asynchronously copies it into the persistent GPU input buffer. CUDA-graph padding extends the buffer without changing the unpadded request semantics.

4.3 Prefill tokens

When a request is still prefilling, prepare_prefill_inputs() gathers the next query tokens from persistent all_token_ids. This gather happens in a Triton kernel so the GPU can read the request state directly, including UVA-backed storage.

4.4 Positions and sequence lengths

prepare_pos_seq_lens() reads the GPU req_states.num_computed_tokens.gpu and writes:

position[b, j] = num_computed_tokens[state_slot] + j
seq_lens[b]    = num_computed_tokens[state_slot] + query_len[b]

The host also builds seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound from the scheduler-side mirror:

num_computed_tokens_np = (
    self.req_states.num_computed_tokens_np[idx_mapping_np]
)
seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound_np = np.zeros(num_reqs_padded, dtype=np.int32)
np.add(
    num_computed_tokens_np,
    num_scheduled_tokens,
    out=seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound_np[:num_reqs],
)

See model_runner.py:1059.

This CPU value is a planning upper bound. It avoids a GPU-to-CPU readback on the common path. It can be optimistic for asynchronous speculative decoding, where the host does not yet know which draft tokens will be rejected.

4.5 Sampled and draft tokens

For autoregressive decode, the input can contain:

  1. The previous sampled token.
  2. Scheduled draft tokens.
  3. A target-model bonus position.

combine_sampled_and_draft_tokens() writes those token IDs into the right input positions and returns logits_indices, which identifies the hidden-state rows that should produce logits.

4.6 Result

The method packages all of these views and mappings in InputBatch, including:

  • input_ids, positions, and is_padding.
  • query_start_loc and seq_lens.
  • seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound.
  • logits_indices and cumulative logit ranges.
  • Prefill flags and prompt lengths.

The optional PCP manager may then partition the batch before returning it.

5. prepare_attn

prepare_attn() turns request indices and positions into paged-attention metadata.

For the normal path it:

  1. Gathers each request’s persistent block-table row into the current batch order.
  2. Computes a slot mapping for each scheduled token.
  3. Returns block tables and slot mappings for all KV-cache groups.
block_tables = self.block_tables.gather_block_tables(
    input_batch.idx_mapping,
    num_reqs_padded=input_batch.num_reqs_after_padding,
)
slot_mappings = self.block_tables.compute_slot_mappings(
    input_batch.idx_mapping,
    input_batch.query_start_loc,
    input_batch.positions,
    num_tokens_padded=input_batch.num_tokens_after_padding,
)

See model_runner.py:1113.

block_tables answer “which physical KV blocks belong to each request?”; slot_mappings answer “which physical KV slot corresponds to each query token?” The attention backend consumes both.

PCP has a specialized preparation path because the logical batch is partitioned before attention metadata is built. Dummy attention metadata is used for profiling and CUDA-graph capture.

6. dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp

dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp() combines two decisions:

  1. Select a compatible CUDA-graph descriptor locally.
  2. Make the execution shape consistent across data-parallel ranks.

For a single DP rank, it simply returns the local descriptor. With multiple DP ranks, sync_cudagraph_and_dp_padding() performs an all-reduce over a small CPU tensor containing:

per-rank token count
per-rank requested CUDA-graph mode
per-rank uniform token count

The synchronization rules are:

  • If all ranks have zero tokens, all ranks skip the forward.
  • If any rank requires eager mode, all ranks use eager mode.
  • Otherwise, the maximum token count is used for a common padded descriptor.
  • Uniform decode is retained only if all ranks agree on the uniform count.

The core logic is in dp_utils.py:16. The resulting num_tokens_across_dp is passed to set_forward_context() so DP-aware kernels know the common execution size.

7. sample_tokens

sample_tokens() consumes the ExecuteModelState produced by the preceding forward.

7.1 Non-last pipeline ranks

Earlier pipeline ranks do not have final hidden states. They receive sampled tokens from the last rank through PPHandler:

all_decode_next = self.pp_handler.receive(input_batch)
self.postprocess_num_computed_tokens(input_batch)

The initial update is optimistic. A later deferred postprocess_sampled() call applies the exact rejection correction when the broadcasted result is consumed. See model_runner.py:1472.

7.2 Last pipeline rank

The last rank:

  1. Restores the original PCP batch if PCP was used.
  2. Selects hidden states at input_batch.logits_indices.
  3. Computes logits.
  4. Applies structured-output grammar masks.
  5. Runs normal sampling or speculative rejection sampling.
  6. Broadcasts sampled tokens and acceptance counts to earlier PP ranks.
  7. Computes prompt logprobs.
  8. Creates AsyncOutput for an overlapping output copy.
  9. Calls postprocess_sampled().
  10. Runs the speculative drafter, if configured.
  11. Performs KV-connector post-forward work.

The sampling decision is implemented by sample():

sample_hidden_states = hidden_states[input_batch.logits_indices]
logits = self.model.compute_logits(sample_hidden_states)

if grammar_output is not None:
    self.structured_outputs_worker.apply_grammar_bitmask(...)

if input_batch.num_draft_tokens == 0:
    sampler_output = self.sampler(logits, input_batch)
else:
    sampler_output = self.rejection_sampler(...)

See model_runner.py:1143.

The output copy is launched before request-state postprocessing so that the device-to-host copy can overlap with state updates and speculative drafting:

async_output = AsyncOutput(...)
self.postprocess_sampled(...)

See model_runner.py:1527.

8. postprocess_sampled

postprocess_sampled() updates GPU-side request state after sampling. It calls post_update(), which updates:

  • last_sampled_tokens.
  • all_token_ids.
  • total_len.
  • Sampling penalty counters.
  • num_computed_tokens.gpu.

The computed-token delta is:

scheduled query length - rejected speculative tokens

Then it calls model_state.postprocess_state(), allowing Mamba/hybrid or other model-specific state to advance.

The scheduler’s host-side Request.num_computed_tokens is not read from this GPU tensor. The scheduler already advanced its own counter at schedule time and later reconciles rejected tokens when it processes the returned output.

9. DefaultModelState

GPUModelRunner delegates model-specific behavior to a ModelState object. The selection logic is in model_states/__init__.py:

  1. A model-provided custom state, if available.
  2. EncoderDecoderModelState for cross-attention models.
  3. EncoderOnlyModelState for encoder-only models.
  4. MambaHybridModelState for hybrid models.
  5. DefaultModelState otherwise.

DefaultModelState handles the common decoder-only path. It owns or coordinates:

  • RoPE position state.
  • Optional multimodal embedding pruning.
  • Multimodal encoder execution and embedding assembly.
  • Model-specific position overrides.
  • Common attention metadata construction.

DefaultModelState.prepare_attn

The method first chooses padded or unpadded dimensions:

if cudagraph_mode == CUDAGraphMode.FULL:
    num_reqs = input_batch.num_reqs_after_padding
    num_tokens = input_batch.num_tokens_after_padding
else:
    num_reqs = input_batch.num_reqs
    num_tokens = input_batch.num_tokens

It then prepares both host and device query offsets:

query_start_loc_cpu = torch.from_numpy(
    input_batch.query_start_loc_np[: num_reqs + 1]
)
query_start_loc_gpu = input_batch.query_start_loc[: num_reqs + 1]

For normal execution, max_seq_len is derived from the CPU upper bound. During capture, it uses max_model_len so the graph remains valid for later replays.

Finally, it calls build_attn_metadata() with both forms of sequence metadata:

attn_metadata = build_attn_metadata(
    ...,
    query_start_loc_gpu=query_start_loc_gpu,
    query_start_loc_cpu=query_start_loc_cpu,
    seq_lens=input_batch.seq_lens,
    max_seq_len=max_seq_len,
    seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound=seq_lens_cpu_upper_bound,
    dcp_local_seq_lens=input_batch.dcp_local_seq_lens,
    positions=input_batch.positions,
    is_prefilling=torch.from_numpy(input_batch.is_prefilling_np),
    ...,
)

See default.py:135 and attn_utils.py:500.

build_attn_metadata() creates a CommonAttentionMetadata object for each KV cache group and invokes that group’s backend metadata builder. The GPU seq_lens is available for device-side execution; the CPU upper bound supports host-side planning such as maximum context lengths and DCP decisions.

10. Triton kernels in input_batch.py

The kernels in input_batch.py move per-step input preparation and state updates onto the GPU. They are not separate model stages; they prepare the buffers consumed by the model and sampler.

10.1 prepare_prefill_inputs

For each batch request, the kernel:

  1. Maps the batch row to a persistent request slot.
  2. Reads num_computed_tokens and prefill_len.
  3. Copies the next query range from all_token_ids into input_ids.
  4. Stores a small lookahead window in next_prefill_tokens for MTP/speculative modules.

This is a straightforward indexed gather; the Triton version avoids a Python loop and can read UVA-backed token history.

10.2 prepare_pos_seq_lens

For each request row it computes positions and the total sequence length after the current query. It also zeros unused rows for FULL CUDA graphs.

A readable, unoptimized reference implementation is:

def prepare_pos_seq_lens_ref(
    idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,          # [num_reqs], device
    query_start_loc: torch.Tensor,      # [num_reqs + 1], device
    num_computed_tokens: torch.Tensor,  # [max_num_reqs], device
    positions: torch.Tensor,            # [max_num_tokens], device
    seq_lens: torch.Tensor,             # [max_num_reqs], device
) -> None:
    num_reqs = idx_mapping.shape[0]

    for batch_idx in range(num_reqs):
        state_idx = int(idx_mapping[batch_idx])
        start = int(query_start_loc[batch_idx])
        end = int(query_start_loc[batch_idx + 1])
        query_len = end - start
        computed = int(num_computed_tokens[state_idx])

        positions[start:end] = torch.arange(
            computed,
            computed + query_len,
            device=positions.device,
            dtype=positions.dtype,
        )
        seq_lens[batch_idx] = computed + query_len

    # Required by FULL CUDA-graph replay.
    seq_lens[num_reqs:] = 0

The production kernel is _prepare_pos_seq_lens_kernel() at input_batch.py:267.

10.3 combine_sampled_and_draft_tokens

This kernel handles the non-contiguous relationship between model input tokens and logits during speculative decoding. It:

  • Computes the positions of the final target/draft logits.
  • Writes the previous sampled token into the first generated-token position.
  • Writes draft tokens into the subsequent positions.
  • Returns the hidden-state indices that should be passed to compute_logits().

For a single request, the conceptual operation is:

def combine_sampled_and_draft_tokens_ref(
    input_ids: torch.Tensor,
    last_sampled_token: int,
    draft_tokens: torch.Tensor,
    query_start: int,
    query_end: int,
    seq_len: int,
    prefill_len: int,
    num_new_sampled_tokens: int = 1,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    num_draft = draft_tokens.numel()
    num_logits = num_new_sampled_tokens + num_draft
    logits_start = query_end - num_logits
    logits_indices = torch.arange(
        logits_start, query_end, device=input_ids.device
    )

    # During decode, the first generated-token input is the previous sample.
    first_logit_seq_pos = seq_len - num_logits
    if (
        num_new_sampled_tokens > 0
        and first_logit_seq_pos >= prefill_len
    ):
        input_ids[logits_start] = last_sampled_token

    if num_draft > 0:
        input_ids[query_end - num_draft:query_end] = draft_tokens

    return logits_indices

The actual implementation supports ragged batches and writes all per-request logit indices into one contiguous tensor. See input_batch.py:325.

10.4 post_update

post_update() applies the result of sampling back to persistent GPU state. For each request it:

  1. Stores the final sampled token as last_sampled_tokens.
  2. Appends sampled tokens to all_token_ids.
  3. Increments total_len by the number of sampled tokens.
  4. Updates penalty counters.
  5. Advances num_computed_tokens by query length minus rejected draft tokens.

The following reference implementation omits Triton parallelism and CUDA-stream details but mirrors the state transitions:

def post_update_ref(
    idx_mapping: torch.Tensor,          # [num_reqs]
    num_computed_tokens: torch.Tensor,  # [max_num_reqs]
    last_sampled_tokens: torch.Tensor,  # [max_num_reqs, 1]
    sampled_tokens: torch.Tensor,       # [num_reqs, max_sample_len]
    num_sampled: torch.Tensor,          # [num_reqs]
    num_rejected: torch.Tensor,         # [num_reqs]
    query_start_loc: torch.Tensor,      # [num_reqs + 1]
    all_token_ids: torch.Tensor,        # [max_num_reqs, max_model_len]
    total_len: torch.Tensor,            # [max_num_reqs]
) -> None:
    for batch_idx in range(idx_mapping.shape[0]):
        state_idx = int(idx_mapping[batch_idx])
        if state_idx < 0:
            continue

        n_sampled = int(num_sampled[batch_idx])
        n_rejected = int(num_rejected[batch_idx])
        old_total_len = int(total_len[state_idx])

        if n_sampled > 0:
            tokens = sampled_tokens[batch_idx, :n_sampled]
            all_token_ids[
                state_idx, old_total_len:old_total_len + n_sampled
            ] = tokens
            last_sampled_tokens[state_idx, 0] = tokens[-1]
            total_len[state_idx] = old_total_len + n_sampled

        query_len = int(
            query_start_loc[batch_idx + 1] - query_start_loc[batch_idx]
        )
        num_computed_tokens[state_idx] += query_len - n_rejected

The production kernel is _post_update_kernel() at input_batch.py:480.

10.5 post_update_num_computed_tokens

This simpler kernel only adds each row’s query length to the GPU computed-token counter. It is used for pooling and for the optimistic non-last-PP path, where the exact sampled/rejected result is applied later:

num_computed_tokens[state_idx] += query_start_loc[i + 1] - query_start_loc[i]

See input_batch.py:582 and model_runner.py:1646.

11. Asynchronous computed-token synchronization

The scheduler and worker do not synchronize by reading the GPU counter back to the CPU. Instead:

Scheduler schedules batch i
  -> host num_computed_tokens advances optimistically
  -> SchedulerOutput carries the old starting count to the worker
  -> GPU prepares positions/seq_lens from its GPU counter
  -> GPU postprocess advances its GPU counter
  -> sampled output returns to the scheduler
  -> scheduler rolls back rejected/stale speculative tokens

The scheduler therefore has a reconciled prefix followed by an optimistic in-flight suffix. With a queue size of two, when scheduling batch i+2, batch i is normally already reconciled while batch i+1 may still be optimistic. With a larger queue, multiple later batches may remain optimistic.

This design preserves overlap while keeping the GPU’s execution state exact. The host-side num_computed_tokens is authoritative for scheduling decisions; the runner-side GPU tensor is authoritative for the currently executing GPU metadata and model state.

12. Suggested reading order

For a new code reader, the following order is effective:

  1. GPUModelRunner.__init__() to see persistent components.
  2. execute_model() for the complete forward lifecycle.
  3. prepare_inputs() and InputBatch for batch layout.
  4. prepare_attn() and DefaultModelState.prepare_attn() for attention metadata.
  5. dispatch_cg_and_sync_dp() for execution-shape coordination.
  6. sample_tokens() and postprocess_sampled() for sampling and state advancement.
  7. input_batch.py for the GPU kernels that connect request state to model inputs and outputs.

chunk_kda_fwd Kernel Walkthrough

A kernel-by-kernel analysis of chunk_kda_fwd (fla/ops/kda/chunk_fwd.py:20), focused on the KDA path and context parallelism (CP). For each Triton kernel: a reference torch implementation, input/output shapes, and the grid layout.

Notation and global shapes

  • $q, k \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times H \times K}$ — queries/keys, $H$ q/k heads, head dim $K$
  • $v \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times H_V \times V}$ — values, $H_V = H \cdot G$ value heads (GQA group size $G$), value dim $V$
  • $g \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times H_V \times K}$ — per-channel log-decay gate (per value head)
  • $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times H_V}$ — delta-rule write strength
  • $\text{BT} = \text{chunk\_size}$ (default 64), $\text{BC} = 16$ (sub-chunk), $\text{NC} = \text{BT}/\text{BC}$ (4 when BT=64)
  • $\text{RCP\_LN2} = 1/\ln 2$ — scaling that turns $\exp(\cdot)$ into $\exp_2(\cdot)$ for kernel speed

The KDA recurrence being chunked is (per value head, dropping batch):

$$ S_t = \exp(g_t) \odot S_{t-1} + \beta_t \, k_t \otimes \bigl(v_t - k_t^\top S_{t-1}\bigr), \qquad o_t = q_t^\top S_t $$

where $\odot$ is element-wise (channel-wise) gate, $\otimes$ is the outer product $k \otimes v = k v^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times V}$.

1. Gate preparation — one of two paths

1a. use_gate_in_kernel=True → kda_gate_chunk_cumsum_vector_kernel

File: fla/ops/kda/gate.py:375. Fuses activation + bias + chunk-local cumsum.

Torch reference

# g_raw: [B, T, H, K], A_log: [H], dt_bias: [H*K] or None
g = g_raw + dt_bias.view(H, K) if dt_bias is not None else g_raw
g = -A_log.exp().view(H, 1) * F.softplus(g)        # [B, T, H, K], in log2 space
g = g * RCP_LN2                                    # convert to log2 base
# chunk-local cumsum along T with chunk_size=BT
g = g.view(B, NT, BT, H, K).cumsum(dim=2).view(B, T, H, K)

Mathematical formula

$$ g_{t,k} \leftarrow \frac{1}{\ln 2} \sum_{\tau = \lfloor t/\text{BT}\rfloor \cdot \text{BT}}^{t} -\exp(A_{\text{log}}) \cdot \text{softplus}(g_{\tau,k} + b_k) $$

Shapes — in: $g[B,T,H,K],\; A_{\text{log}}[H],\; dt\_bias[H*K]?$; out: $g[B,T,H,K]$ (fp32).

Grid: (cdiv(K, BS), NT, B*H) — i_s tiles the $K$ dim, i_t is the chunk, i_bh is batch×head. Each program computes a $[\text{BT}, \text{BS}]$ tile, applies bias and $-\exp(A_{\text{log}}) \cdot \text{softplus}(\cdot)$, then tl.cumsum along the BT axis.

1b. use_gate_in_kernel=False (default) → chunk_local_cumsum_vector_kernel

File: fla/ops/utils/cumsum.py:90. Skips activation — assumes g is already the log-decay; just rescales by $\text{RCP\_LN2}$ and chunk-cumsums.

Torch reference

g = (g * RCP_LN2).view(B, NT, BT, H, K).cumsum(dim=2).view(B, T, H, K)

Mathematical formula

$$ g_{t,k} \leftarrow \frac{1}{\ln 2} \sum_{\tau = \lfloor t/\text{BT}\rfloor \cdot \text{BT}}^{t} g_{\tau,k} $$

Shapes — in/out: $[B, T, H, K]$ (here $H$ is $H_V$ because $g$ has value-head dim).

Grid: (cdiv(S, BS), NT, B*H) with $S = K$. Same tiling as 1a but no activation, just tl.cumsum and scale.

2. Intra-chunk: chunk_kda_fwd_intra (fla/ops/kda/chunk_intra.py:818)

Returns $w, u, q_g, k_g, A_{qk}, A_{kk}$. Internally calls three Triton kernels.

2a. Diagonal sub-blocks — chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_token_parallel (default) or chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_sub_chunk (safe_gate)

These compute the diagonal $\text{BC} \times \text{BC}$ blocks of the intra-chunk attention matrices:

  • $A_{qk}[i, j] = \text{scale} \cdot (q_i \odot \exp(g_i - g_j)) \cdot k_j$ for $j \le i$ (lower-triangular), diagonal sub-chunks only
  • $A_{kk}[i, j] = \beta_i \cdot (k_i \odot \exp(g_i - g_j)) \cdot k_j$ for $j < i$ (strictly lower, since diagonal is consumed by the solve)

The $A_{kk}$ diagonal blocks are stored separately in Akkd (fp32) for precision during the triangular solve.

Torch reference (matches the loop in naive_chunk_kda, fla/ops/kda/naive.py:127-136)

# A_qq: [B, HV, NT, BT, BT] (only diagonal BC-blocks filled)
# A_kk: [B, HV, NT, BT, BC] (only the strictly-lower part of the diagonal BC-block, fp32)
for i in range(BT):
    k_i = k[..., i, :]
    g_i = g[..., i:i+1, :]
    Aqk_diag[..., i] = (q * exp(g - g_i)).sum(-1) @ k_i.T   # only j in same sub-chunk
    Akk_diag[..., i] = (k * exp(g - g_i)).sum(-1) @ k_i.T * beta[..., i]
Akk_diag = Akk_diag.masked_fill(mask_upper_or_diag, 0)

Mathematical formula (for tokens $i, j$ in the same sub-chunk)

$$ A_{qk}[i, j] = \begin{cases} \text{scale} \cdot \sum_d q_{i,d} \, k_{j,d} \, \exp_2(g_{i,d} - g_{j,d}) & j \le i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$$$ A_{kk}[i, j] = \begin{cases} \beta_i \cdot \sum_d k_{i,d} \, k_{j,d} \, \exp_2(g_{i,d} - g_{j,d}) & j < i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

The kernel then computes the diagonal inverse $(I + \text{tril}(A_{kk}^{\text{diag}}))^{-1}$ via forward substitution in registers.

Shapes:

  • in: $q, k, g_k[B, T, H/H_V, K]$, $\beta[B, T, H_V]$, $\text{scale}$
  • out: $A_{qk}[B, T, H_V, \text{BT}]$ (lower-triangular row of the chunk matrix, q.dtype), $A_{kkd}[B, T, H_V, \text{BC}]$ (fp32)

Grid for chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_token_parallel (fla/ops/kda/chunk_intra_token_parallel.py:33): (B*T, cdiv(HV, BH)) — one program per (token, head-group). Each program loads $q_t, k_t, \beta_t$ and loops over $j$ from sub-chunk start to $i_t$, doing one token row of $A_{qk}$/$A_{kk}$. This “token-parallel” layout avoids wasted compute on padded tokens in varlen.

Grid for chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_sub_chunk (fla/ops/kda/chunk_intra.py:683): (NT, NC, B*HV) — one program per (chunk, sub-chunk, batch×value-head). Loads a $[\text{BC}, \text{BK}]$ tile of $q, k, g$, computes $b_{A_{qk}} = (q \odot g_q) \cdot (k \odot g_k)^\top \cdot \text{scale}$, $b_{A_{kk}} = (k \odot g_q) \cdot (k \odot g_k)^\top \cdot \beta$, masks to lower-triangular, writes to $A_{qk}$/$A_{kkd}$, then runs an in-register forward-substitution to invert $(I + \text{tril}(A_{kk}))$ for this BC-block. Uses gather for the reference gate row when hardware supports it (numerical stability).

2b. Off-diagonal blocks + merged inverse — chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_inter_solve_fused

File: fla/ops/kda/chunk_intra.py:43. Computes the off-diagonal $A_{qk}$ and $A_{kk}$ sub-blocks (within a chunk, across the $\text{NC}=4$ sub-chunks), then assembles the merged inverse $(I + \text{tril}(A_{kk}^{\text{chunk}}))^{-1}$ block-by-block using the already-inverted diagonal blocks loaded from Akkd.

Torch reference (continuing naive_chunk_kda)

# Off-diagonal sub-blocks (i_s > j_s)
for i_s in range(NC):
    for j_s in range(i_s):
        Aqk_chunk[:, i_s*BC:(i_s+1)*BC, j_s*BC:(j_s+1)*BC] = (
            q_blk_i * exp(g_i - g_j)) @ k_blk_j.T * scale
        )
        Akk_chunk[:, i_s*BC:(i_s+1)*BC, j_s*BC:(j_s+1)*BC] = (
            k_blk_i * exp(g_i - g_j)) @ k_blk_j.T * beta_i
        )

# Forward-substitution inverse of (I + tril(Akk_chunk)) — block-triangular inverse formula
Akk_inv = block_tril_inverse(Akk_chunk, Akkd_inv)  # see lines 269-351

Mathematical formula (block-triangular inverse for $\text{NC}=4$ sub-chunks, denoting $A_{kk}^{ij}$ the $(i, j)$ sub-block):

$$ \begin{aligned} A_{kk}^{-1,00} &= (I + A_{kk}^{00})^{-1} \quad \text{(from Akkd)} \\ A_{kk}^{-1,11} &= (I + A_{kk}^{11})^{-1} \quad \text{(from Akkd)} \\ A_{kk}^{-1,10} &= -A_{kk}^{-1,11} \, A_{kk}^{10} \, A_{kk}^{-1,00} \\ A_{kk}^{-1,21} &= -A_{kk}^{-1,22} \, A_{kk}^{21} \, A_{kk}^{-1,11} \\ A_{kk}^{-1,20} &= -A_{kk}^{-1,22} \bigl( A_{kk}^{20} A_{kk}^{-1,00} + A_{kk}^{21} A_{kk}^{-1,10} \bigr) \\ A_{kk}^{-1,30} &= -A_{kk}^{-1,33} \bigl( A_{kk}^{30} A_{kk}^{-1,00} + A_{kk}^{31} A_{kk}^{-1,10} + A_{kk}^{32} A_{kk}^{-1,20} \bigr) \\ &\;\;\vdots \end{aligned} $$

Shapes:

  • in: $q, k, g_k, \beta$, $A_{kkd}[B, T, H_V, \text{BC}]$ (fp32, diagonal inverses from 2a)
  • out: $A_{qk}[B, T, H_V, \text{BT}]$ (now full chunk matrix, q.dtype), $A_{kk}[B, T, H_V, \text{BT}]$ (full inverse, q.dtype)

Grid: (NT, B*HV) — one program per (chunk, batch×value-head). Each program:

  1. Loops $i_k$ over $K$-tiles, accumulates the 6 (NC=4 → 6) off-diagonal $\text{BC} \times \text{BC}$ blocks of $A_{qk}$ and $A_{kk}$ in registers.
  2. Stores off-diag $A_{qk}$ blocks to global, multiplies off-diag $A_{kk}$ blocks by $\beta$.
  3. Loads the 4 diagonal $A_{kk}^{-1}$ blocks from $A_{kkd}$ (fp32).
  4. Combines them with the merged inverse formula above using tf32 precision (lines 315-351).
  5. Stores the full $A_{kk}$ inverse to global.

2c. WY representation — recompute_w_u_fwd_kda_kernel

File: fla/ops/kda/wy_fast.py:34. Builds the WY factorization needed for the inter-chunk recurrence:

  • $u = A \cdot v$ where $A = (I + \text{tril}(A_{kk}))^{-1}$ (computed above)
  • $w = A \cdot (\beta \odot k \odot \exp(g))$ (gated, beta-scaled keys)
  • $k_g = k \odot \exp(g_{\text{last}} - g)$ (key aligned to chunk-end for the state update)
  • $q_g = q \odot \exp(g)$ (optional, only if disable_recompute=True)

Torch reference (naive_chunk_kda lines 138-139)

A_inv = Akk                                              # [B, HV, NT, BT, BT]
w = A_inv @ (exp(g) * k)                                 # [B, HV, NT, BT, K]
u = A_inv @ v                                            # [B, HV, NT, BT, V]
qg = q * exp(g)                                          # optional
kg = k * exp(g_last - g)                                 # for state update

Mathematical formula

$$ u_t = \sum_{j \le t} A_{kk}^{-1}[t, j] \, v_j, \qquad w_t = \sum_{j \le t} A_{kk}^{-1}[t, j] \, \beta_j \, k_j \, \exp_2(g_j) $$$$ k_{g,t} = k_t \odot \exp_2(g_{\text{last}} - g_t), \qquad q_{g,t} = q_t \odot \exp_2(g_t) $$

Shapes:

  • in: $k[B, T, H, K]$, $v[B, T, H_V, V]$, $\beta[B, T, H_V]$, $A = A_{kk}[B, T, H_V, \text{BT}]$, $g_k[B, T, H_V, K]$, optional $q$
  • out: $w[B, T, H_V, K]$, $u[B, T, H_V, V]$ (alias for v_new later), $k_g[B, T, H_V, K]$, $q_g[B, T, H_V, K]?$

Grid: (NT, B*HV). Each program loops over BT rows of $A$, computes $u = A \cdot (\beta_v \odot v)$ for BV-tiles of $V$, then $w = A \cdot (\beta \odot k \odot \exp(g))$ for BK-tiles of $K$ (lines 92-128). Same program writes $q_g$ and $k_g$ if requested.

3. CP pre-processing — only when cp_context is not None

chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_pre_process (fla/ops/cp/chunk_delta_h.py:747) builds the initial state for this rank by gathering per-rank chunk-summary matrices from earlier ranks. It uses two Triton kernels plus an all-gather.

3a. pre_process_fwd_kernel_merged (skip on is_last_rank)

File: fla/ops/cp/chunk_delta_h.py:41. Each rank computes a per-rank summary $(h_{\text{rank}}, M_{\text{rank}})$ of shape $[H_V, K, V+K]$, where:

  • $h_{\text{rank}}$ (the $[:, :, :V]$ part) is the “forced” state contribution of this rank’s tokens assuming $h_0 = 0$:
$$ h_{\text{rank}} = \sum_t k_t^\top \bigl(v_t - w_t \, h_{t-1}\bigr) \cdot \exp_2(g_{\text{last}} - g_t) $$
  • $M_{\text{rank}}$ (the $[:, :, V:]$ part, $K \times K$) is the chunked transition matrix:
$$ M_{\text{rank}} = \prod_t \bigl(\text{diag}(\exp_2(g_{\text{last}})) - k_t^\top w_t\bigr) $$

$M_{\text{rank}}$ propagates an arbitrary $h_0$ through this rank’s tokens.

Torch reference (conceptual)

# h0 arbitrary; for the rank starting fresh, h0=0
h = h0                                              # [HV, K, V]
M = eye(K)                                          # [HV, K, K]
for chunk in rank_chunks:
    v_new = v_chunk - w_chunk @ h                   # delta-rule update
    v_new *= exp(g_last - g_chunk)                  # gate-align to chunk end
    h = h * exp(g_last) + k_chunk.T @ v_new         # state update
    M = (diag(exp(g_last)) - k_chunk.T @ w_chunk) @ M
# Output: hm[:, :, :V] = h, hm[:, :, V:] = M  (per rank, [HV, K, V+K])

Shapes:

  • in: $k, w, u, g_k$ (only last sequence via cu_seqlens[-2:]), $\text{bg} = \text{None}$ for KDA (KDA path uses USE_GK=True, USE_BG=False)
  • out: $h_m[H_V, K, V+K]$ (fp32)

Grid: (cdiv(V, BLOCK_SIZE) + cdiv(K, BLOCK_SIZE), HV). Each program handles either the $h$ part ($i_{\text{col}} < \text{cdiv}(V, \text{BS})$, computes a $[64, \text{BLOCK\_SIZE}]$ tile of $h$ via the recurrence) or the $M$ part ($i_{\text{col}} \ge \text{cdiv}(V, \text{BS})$, computes a $[\text{BK1}, \text{BLOCK\_SIZE}]$ tile of $M$). Note $\text{BK1} = \text{next\_power\_of\_2}(K)$.

3b. all_gather_into_tensor

A torch.distributed collective (not Triton) — gathers $h_m$ across all CP ranks into $ag_{hm}[\text{world\_size}, H_V, K, V+K]$. See fla/ops/cp/comm.py.

3c. merge_fwd_bwd_kernel with FORWARD=True (skip on is_first_rank)

File: fla/ops/cp/chunk_delta_h.py:332. Folds the per-rank summaries from all preceding ranks into this rank’s initial_state.

Torch reference

# h0 for this rank = composition of all previous ranks' (h_rank, M_rank)
h = zeros(HV, K, V)
for prev_rank in ranks_before_me:
    h_prev, M_prev = ag_hm[prev_rank]              # h_prev: [K, V], M_prev: [K, K]
    h = M_prev @ h + h_prev                        # fold previous rank's contribution
initial_state[0] = h                               # [N=1, HV, K, V]

Mathematical formula

$$ h_0^{(\text{this rank})} = \sum_{r \in \text{prev\_ranks}} \left( \prod_{r' \le r} M_{r'} \right) h_r \;=\; M_{r_1} h_{r_0} + M_{r_2}(M_{r_1} h_{r_0} + h_{r_1}) + \cdots $$

Iteratively: $h \leftarrow M_r \, h + h_r$ for each previous rank $r$ in order.

Shapes:

  • in: $ag_{hm}[\text{world\_size}, H_V, K, V+K]$, $\text{pre\_num\_ranks}$, $\text{rank}$
  • out: $\text{initial\_state}[N, H_V, K, V]$ (or $[N, H_V, V, K]$ if state_v_first)

Grid (CP mode): (cdiv(V, BV), HV) — $i_v$ tiles $V$, $i_h$ is the head. Each program loops over $\text{pre\_num\_ranks}$ previous ranks, loads $(h_{\text{prev}}, M_{\text{prev}})$ tiles, and accumulates $h = M_{\text{prev}} \, h + h_{\text{prev}}$ (line 441-453). When state_v_first=True the layout is transposed: $h^\top{}' = h^\top \, M^\top + h_{\text{prev}}^\top$.

3d. compress_h0 (fla/ops/cp/chunk_delta_h.py:923) — pure torch

Returns initial_state[:1].clone(). Only the first sequence in the local batch can be a CP continuation, so the rest is dropped to save memory for save_for_backward. No kernel.

4. Inter-chunk state recurrence — chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h

File: fla/ops/common/chunk_delta_h.py:50, kernel chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_kernel_h_blockdim64. Computes the per-chunk hidden states $h[0 \ldots \text{NT}-1]$ and $v_{\text{new}}$ (the delta-rule-corrected values), using the initial_state from step 3 (or the user-supplied one in non-CP mode).

Torch reference (matches naive_chunk_kda lines 160-163)

S = initial_state                                  # [N, HV, K, V]
v_new_chunks = []
for i in range(NT):
    v_new = u_i - w_i @ S                          # delta-rule: subtract predicted from v
    v_new_gated = v_new * exp(g_last_i - g_i)      # align to chunk end
    h[i] = S                                       # store state at chunk start
    S = S * exp(g_last_i) + k_i.T @ v_new_gated    # state update with gated new value
final_state = S

Mathematical formula (per chunk $i$, with $S$ the running state)

$$ v_{\text{new}}^{(i)} = u^{(i)} - w^{(i)} \, S_{i-1} $$$$ \tilde{v}^{(i)}_t = v_{\text{new},t}^{(i)} \odot \exp_2(g_{\text{last}}^{(i)} - g_t) $$$$ S_i = \text{diag}(\exp_2(g_{\text{last}}^{(i)})) \, S_{i-1} + k^{(i)\,\top} \, \tilde{v}^{(i)} $$$$ h[i] = S_{i-1}, \qquad \text{final\_state} = S_{\text{NT}} $$

Shapes:

  • in: $k[B, T, H, K]$, $w[B, T, H_V, K]$, $u[B, T, H_V, V]$, $g[B, T, H_V]?$, $g_k[B, T, H_V, K]?$, $\text{initial\_state}[N, H_V, K, V]?$
  • out: $h[B, \text{NT}, H_V, K, V]$ (or $[B, \text{NT}, H_V, V, K]$ if state_v_first), $v_{\text{new}}[B, T, H_V, V]$, $\text{final\_state}[N, H_V, K, V]?$

Grid: (cdiv(V, BV) * N * HV,) — one program per (V-tile, sequence, head). Each program iterates NT chunks, maintaining 1-4 register tiles of size $[64, \text{BV}]$ (one per 64-wide $K$ slice, since $K \le 256$). Per chunk: stores current $h$ tile, computes $v_{\text{new}} = u - w \, h$, applies gate decay $\exp_2(g_{\text{last}} - g)$, decays $h$ by $\exp_2(g_{\text{last}})$ and $\exp_2(g_{k,\text{last}})$ (per-channel), then $h \mathrel{+}= k^\top v_{\text{new}}$. Final chunk’s $h$ is stored to final_state.

5. Output projection — chunk_gla_fwd_o_gk → chunk_gla_fwd_kernel_o

File: fla/ops/gla/chunk.py:345. Computes the final attention output by combining the inter-chunk state contribution and the intra-chunk attention.

Torch reference (naive_chunk_kda line 161)

# o_i = (q_i * exp(g_i)) @ h[i] + Aqk_i @ v_new_i
o = (qg @ h_inter) + Aqk @ v_new                  # [B, HV, NT, BT, V]

Mathematical formula

$$ o^{(i)} = \bigl(q^{(i)} \odot \exp_2(g^{(i)})\bigr) \, h[i] \cdot \text{scale} + A_{qk}^{(i)} \, v_{\text{new}}^{(i)} $$

Shapes:

  • in: $q[B, T, H, K]$, $v = v_{\text{new}}[B, T, H_V, V]$, $g[B, T, H_V, K]$, $A = A_{qk}[B, T, H_V, \text{BT}]$, $h[B, \text{NT}, H_V, K, V]$, $\text{scale}$
  • out: $o[B, T, H_V, V]$ (zeros-initialized — vLLM pads $v$)

Grid: (cdiv(V, BV), NT, B*HV) — $i_v$ tiles $V$, $i_t$ is the chunk, $i_{bh}$ is batch×value-head. Each program:

  1. Loops $i_k$ over $K$-tiles, loads $q, g, h$ tiles, accumulates $b_o = (q \odot \exp_2(g)) \, h$.
  2. Multiplies by $\text{scale}$.
  3. Loads $v_{\text{new}}$ and the lower-triangular $A_{qk}$ row for this chunk, adds $A_{qk} \, v_{\text{new}}$.
  4. Stores $o$.

Summary of program-division patterns

Kernel Grid Per-program tile
kda_gate_chunk_cumsum_vector_kernel (cdiv(K,BS), NT, B*H) $[\text{BT}, \text{BS}]$ gate tile
chunk_local_cumsum_vector_kernel (cdiv(K,BS), NT, B*H) $[\text{BT}, \text{BS}]$ gate tile
chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_token_parallel (B*T, cdiv(HV,BH)) one token row, $\text{BH}$ heads
chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_intra_sub_chunk (NT, NC, B*HV) $[\text{BC}, \text{BK}]$ sub-chunk × $K$-tile
chunk_kda_fwd_kernel_inter_solve_fused (NT, B*HV) full $\text{BT} \times \text{BT}$ chunk (4×4 BC blocks)
recompute_w_u_fwd_kda_kernel (NT, B*HV) $\text{BT}$ rows of $w, u, q_g, k_g$
pre_process_fwd_kernel_merged (CP) (cdiv(V,BS)+cdiv(K,BS), HV) $[64, \text{BS}]$ of $h$ or $[\text{BK1}, \text{BS}]$ of $M$
merge_fwd_bwd_kernel (CP) (cdiv(V,BV), HV) $[\text{BK}, \text{BV}]$ tile of initial_state
chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_kernel_h_blockdim64 (cdiv(V,BV)*N*HV,) $[64, \text{BV}]$ state tile, NT-chunk loop
chunk_gla_fwd_kernel_o (cdiv(V,BV), NT, B*HV) $[\text{BT}, \text{BV}]$ output tile

CP flow recap

In non-CP mode, step 3 is skipped and initial_state flows directly from the user into step 4. In CP mode:

  1. Each non-last rank computes its $(h_{\text{rank}}, M_{\text{rank}})$ summary (3a) — $M_{\text{rank}}$ is the linear transfer matrix that propagates any $h_0$ across this rank’s tokens.
  2. Summaries are all-gathered (3b).
  3. Each non-first rank folds all preceding ranks’ summaries into its initial_state (3c) via $h \leftarrow M_r \, h + h_r$.
  4. compress_h0 (3d) trims to a single sequence for backward’s save_for_backward.

This avoids ever materializing or communicating full $[K, V]$ states per chunk across ranks — only one $[K, V+K]$ summary per rank is gathered, giving CP overhead that’s independent of sequence length.

Zhixuan's Blog https://zhixuan-zxli.github.io/llm/mooncake_connector/ -

Mooncake KV Connectors in vLLM

vLLM ships two different KVConnectorBase_V1 implementations for Mooncake, with fundamentally different transfer architectures:

  • MooncakeConnector — direct P2P transfer via RDMA one-sided writes.
  • MooncakeStoreConnector — shared distributed KV pool keyed by content hash.

Source files:

  • vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/mooncake_connector.py
  • vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/connector.py

1. MooncakeConnector — Direct P2P transfer

This is a P-push connector: the producer (prefiller) writes KV blocks directly into the consumer’s (decoder’s) memory via RDMA. It’s built on top of Mooncake’s TransferEngine, which does one-sided RDMA writes.

Architecture

  • Split into MooncakeConnectorScheduler (control-plane) and MooncakeConnectorWorker (data-plane), matching the standard vLLM connector role split.
  • Both P and D workers can coexist in one process (kv_both) — the code branches on is_kv_producer / is_kv_consumer.

Discovery: bootstrap server

  • Global-rank-0 P-worker launches an HTTP MooncakeBootstrapServer.
  • Every P-worker registers (engine_id, dp_rank, tp_rank, pp_rank, zmq_addr) with it.
  • D-workers hit the bootstrap /query endpoint on first contact with a new engine_id (_connect_to_prefiller_bootstrap), caching the topology in _remote_agents.

Metadata channel: ZMQ

  • P-worker binds a ZMQ ROUTER socket to a random port; that port is what gets registered with bootstrap.
  • D-worker uses a DEALER socket to send a MooncakeXferMetadata blob per pull request. That blob contains the D’s KV base addresses, block lengths, per-layer registrations, plus per-request (transfer_id, [[block_ids]]).
  • P responds with MooncakeXferResponse, streamed as CONTINUE messages while transfers finish incrementally and FINISH at the end.

KV registration

register_kv_caches iterates each layer’s KV tensor. Depending on the attention spec:

  • MLA / SlidingWindowMLA → treat whole layer as one region (page_size_bytes).
  • Mamba/GDN → register only the conv tensor.
  • Standard attention with virtually_split_kv_in_blocks layout → treat K and V halves as separate transfer regions (kv_block_len = block_len // 2). _expand_transfer_regions emits two TransferRegion entries per layer, one at base_addr and one at base_addr + kv_block_len.

All unique storage_addr regions are batch-registered with Mooncake’s RDMA layer via engine.batch_register_memory — this is what pins the memory for one-sided RDMA writes.

The actual transfer

_build_transfer_params is where block-level RDMA descriptors are computed:

  1. Group-aware block matching. Hybrid models can have multiple KV groups (e.g. full-attention pages + GDN inner-state slots). Block IDs from group i on P must only be paired with group i on D — the code carefully preserves per-group identity. For Mamba groups, NULL_BLOCK_ID placeholders are filtered out.
  2. Region alignment across PP shards. _align_transfer_regions matches registered regions by (layer_name, occurrence_order) rather than positionally, because P and D may have different PP layouts and thus own different layer subsets.
  3. Heterogeneous TP planning. _compute_sender_transfer_plan figures out, for a given (local_tp_rank, remote_tp_rank) pair:
    • Whether this rank sends at all (for replicated caches like MLA, only rank 0 within a TP group needs to send).
    • Source/dest byte offsets inside a KV block (when local TP > remote TP, one local rank writes into a slice of the remote block; when local TP < remote TP, one local rank gathers from multiple remote regions).
    • tp_ratio handles both directions with sign convention.
  4. Coalescing. group_concurrent_contiguous uses np.diff to find runs of contiguous block IDs on both sides. When a run is contiguous AND the per-block copy covers the full block (_can_coalesce_block_transfers), the whole run becomes one large descriptor instead of N small ones. Big win for RDMA throughput.
  5. Logical → kernel expansion (_logical_to_kernel_block_ids). When speculative decoding forces the effective kernel block size smaller than the logical one, each logical block ID expands to _physical_blocks_per_logical_kv_block consecutive kernel IDs. Mamba groups skip this expansion.
  6. The dispatch: engine.batch_transfer_sync_write(remote_session, src_ptrs, dst_ptrs, lengths). This is the RDMA one-sided WRITE into the D’s registered memory, no D-side CPU involvement.

Async orchestration

  • Two background threads each running their own asyncio event loop (_async_loop): sender loop on P, receiver loop on D.
  • On P, _mooncake_sender_listener accepts ZMQ requests and dispatches to _sender_worker coroutines (num_sender_tasks = 2 × num_workers) which pull from a queue.
  • The actual batch_transfer_sync_write call is offloaded to a ThreadPoolExecutor via run_in_executor since it’s a blocking C call. Each executor thread is bound to the correct CUDA device via _bind_sender_thread_device — CUDA context is thread-local, so this is essential for NVLink transfers on TP > 0.

Special cases

  • Mamba/GDN on the P side truncates the last prompt token (_truncate_mamba_request_for_prefill) so P computes h(N-1), then D recomputes the final token to derive h(N). This avoids sending a state that would need immediate refresh.
  • Sliding-window HMA clips block IDs to the last blocks_per_sw blocks so old windows aren’t wastefully transferred.
  • Timeout handling — SendBlockMeta.expire_time plus fetch_finished_sending_reqs reap stranded P-side blocks if D never asks for them.
  • P/D asymmetry in stats — only P sees successful transfer latency/bytes; D only records recv failures because it never touches the successful path.

KV cache layout

get_required_kvcache_layout returns "HND" for non-MLA models, so layout is forced to [num_heads, num_blocks, block_size, head_dim] and heterogeneous TP transfers are contiguous on the head dimension.

2. Call stacks — Send and receive

One-time worker setup

P-worker __init__                          D-worker __init__
├── threading.Thread(_async_loop,          ├── threading.Thread(_async_loop,
│      sender_loop).start()                │      receiver_loop).start()
└── register_kv_caches(...)                └── register_kv_caches(...)
    ├── engine.batch_register_memory()         └── engine.batch_register_memory()
    │      # pin memory for RDMA
    └── run_coroutine_threadsafe(
           _mooncake_sender_listener, sender_loop)
        ├── sock = ROUTER.bind_to_random_port
        ├── register_worker_with_bootstrap()    ── HTTP ─▶ MooncakeBootstrapServer
        └── spawn N × _sender_worker(sock)

Prefiller (P) — sending KV

─── Scheduler process (SCHEDULER role) ──────────────────────────────────
Engine step
└── connector.update_state_after_alloc(req)
       │   if params["do_remote_decode"]:
       └── self._reqs_need_send[req_id] = (req, [])

Engine step (end)
├── connector.build_connector_meta(sched_out)
│      └── meta.add_new_req(load_remote_cache=False)  ─┐
│                                                      │
└── connector.request_finished(req, block_ids)         │
       │   # request completed on P                    │
       └── self._reqs_need_send[req_id] = (req, block_ids) ─┘
                                                       │
                        MooncakeConnectorMetadata      │
                                                       ▼
─── Worker process (WORKER role) ───────────────────────────────────────
connector.start_load_kv(fwd_ctx)
└── run_coroutine_threadsafe(record_send_reqs, sender_loop)
       └── record_send_reqs(metadata)
              ├── send_meta = SendBlockMeta(...)  ── store in self.reqs_need_send
              └── send_meta.ready.set()          ── unblocks send_kv_to_decode

┌────────────── sender_loop thread (asyncio) ────────────────────────┐
│                                                                    │
│  _mooncake_sender_listener()                                       │
│  └── while True:                                                   │
│      identity, meta_bytes = sock.recv_multipart()  ◀── ZMQ from D  │
│      sender_worker_queue.put(...)                                  │
│                                                                    │
│  _sender_worker(sock)  × num_sender_tasks                          │
│  └── send_kv_to_decode(identity, sock, meta)                       │
│      ├── local_regions  = _get_transfer_regions(local KV)          │
│      ├── remote_regions = _get_transfer_regions(D's KV from meta)  │

│      │                                                             │
│      └── while wait_tasks:                                         │
│           done = await asyncio.wait(ready events, timeout)         │
│           ├── _build_transfer_params(ready_reqs, ...)              │
│           │   ├── filter NULL_BLOCK_ID (Mamba)                     │
│           │   ├── _logical_to_kernel_block_ids()                   │
│           │   ├── group_concurrent_contiguous()  # coalesce runs   │
│           │   ├── _get_sender_transfer_plan()    # het-TP offsets  │
│           │   └── build (src_ptrs, dst_ptrs, lengths)              │
│           │                                                        │
│           ├── run_in_executor(_sender_executor, _send_blocks)      │
│           │   └── ─── ThreadPoolExecutor thread ────────────────┐  │
│           │       │  _send_blocks(remote_session, ptrs, lens)   │  │
│           │       │  └── engine.batch_transfer_sync_write(...)  │  │
│           │       │       # RDMA one-sided WRITEs into D memory │  │
│           │       └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│           │                                                        │
│           ├── mark reqs sent, add to finished_sending_reqs         │
│           └── sock.send_multipart(MooncakeXferResponse)  ──▶ D     │
│                                                                    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

─── back on Worker main thread ─────────────────────────────────────────
connector.get_finished()
└── run_coroutine_threadsafe(fetch_finished_sending_reqs)
       └── returns finished_sending_reqs  ──▶ scheduler frees blocks

Decoder (D) — receiving KV

─── Scheduler process ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Engine step
├── connector.get_num_new_matched_tokens(req)
│      # do_remote_prefill → return (num_prompt_tokens, True)
│
└── connector.update_state_after_alloc(req, blocks, n_ext)
       └── self._reqs_need_recv[req_id] = (req, local_block_ids)

Engine step (end)
└── connector.build_connector_meta(sched_out)
       └── meta.reqs_to_recv[remote_engine_id][req_id] = PullReqMeta(
              transfer_id, local_block_ids, remote_bootstrap_addr)

                        MooncakeConnectorMetadata
                                 │
─── Worker process ──────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────
connector.start_load_kv(fwd_ctx)
└── run_coroutine_threadsafe(_start_load_kv, receiver_loop)

┌────────────── receiver_loop thread (asyncio) ──────────────────────┐
│                                                                    │
│  _start_load_kv(reqs_to_recv)                                      │
│  └── for remote_engine_id, pull_metas:                             │
│      ├── (first time) handle_new_engine_id()                       │
│      │   └── _connect_to_prefiller_bootstrap()   ── HTTP GET ──┐   │
│      │       └── populate self._remote_agents                  │   │
│      │                                                      Bootstrap
│      └── receive_kv(remote_engine_id, pull_metas)                  │
│          ├── remote_tp_ranks = transfer_topo.handshake_target_ranks│
│          ├── select worker_addrs (per remote TP × PP rank)         │
│          └── for worker_addr:                                      │
│              create_task(receive_kv_from_single_worker)            │
│                                                                    │
│  receive_kv_from_single_worker(worker_addr, pull_metas)            │
│  ├── metadata = MooncakeXferMetadata(                              │
│  │       hostname, port, tp_size, tp_rank,                         │
│  │       req_blocks={req_id: (xid, local_block_ids)},              │
│  │       kv_caches_base_addr, block_lens, kv_block_lens,           │
│  │       registered_layer_names/indices/group_indices)             │
│  │                                                                 │
│  ├── sock = DEALER connect(worker_addr)     ── ZMQ ──▶ P sender    │
│  ├── await sock.send(encoded_meta)                                 │
│  │                                                                 │
│  └── while True:                                                   │
│      ret_msg = await sock.recv()  ◀─── MooncakeXferResponse ─── P  │
│      response = decode(ret_msg)                                    │
│      ├── if ERROR: xfer_stats.record_failed_recv(); return         │
│      ├── process_pulling_result(response, pull_metas)              │
│      │   └── for req_id in response.ok_reqs:                       │
│      │       pull_meta.pull_tasks_count -= 1                       │
│      │       if 0: finished_recving_reqs.add(req_id)               │
│      └── if FINISH: break                                          │
│                                                                    │
│  (RDMA WRITE from P has already landed in the registered           │
│   local KV memory before FINISH — nothing to copy on this side)    │
│                                                                    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

─── Worker main thread ────────────────────────────────────────────────
connector.get_finished()
└── run_coroutine_threadsafe(fetch_finished_recving_reqs)
       └── returns finished_recving_reqs  ──▶ scheduler unblocks decode

End-to-end timeline

   D scheduler        D worker (recv loop)     P worker (send loop)     P scheduler
       │                     │                          │                   │
 update_state_after_alloc    │                          │                   │
       │                     │                          │           update_state_after_alloc
 build_connector_meta ──▶ start_load_kv                 │                   │
                             │                          │           build_connector_meta
                             │                       start_load_kv ◀────────┘
                             │                       (record_send_reqs
                             │                        creates SendBlockMeta)
                             │                          │
                       _start_load_kv                   │
                             │                          │
                       handle_new_engine_id             │
                             │─── HTTP /query ────▶ bootstrap
                             │◀───   addrs   ──────────┘
                             │                          │
                     receive_kv_from_single_worker      │
                             │──── ZMQ meta ───────▶ _mooncake_sender_listener
                             │                          │
                             │                    _sender_worker
                             │                    → send_kv_to_decode
                             │                    → _build_transfer_params
                             │                    → _send_blocks
                             │                     ═══ RDMA WRITE ═══▶ D KV memory
                             │◀── ZMQ FINISH ──────────┘
                       process_pulling_result           │
                             │                          │           request_finished (P)
 get_finished                │                          │           (delays free until sent)
  → finished_recving_reqs    │                    finished_sending_reqs
       ◀─────────────────────┘                          └───────────▶ get_finished → free

3. MooncakeStoreConnector — Shared distributed KV pool

Fundamentally different model: instead of P pushing to D, both instances independently read from and write to a MooncakeDistributedStore — a shared KV cache pool indexed by content hash.

Why the two connectors are not interchangeable

  • P2P connector: dedicated P and D roles, one-shot transfer per request, no cross-request reuse across instances.
  • Store connector: any instance can be both producer and consumer. Blocks are keyed by hash, so if two requests share a prefix (even across instances), the second one reads from the store instead of recomputing. This is prefix caching at the fleet level.

Structure

  • Delegates to MooncakeStoreScheduler and MooncakeStoreWorker. The connector file is mostly a thin dispatcher.
  • No layerwise saving/loading (save_kv_layer / wait_for_layer_load are no-ops). Puts and gets are batched and issued from get_finished for compute overlap.

Prefix-cache reset

reset_cache drains the send queue then calls remove_all on the Mooncake master. Caller must pause generation first so nothing races in during drain. Only meaningful on the scheduler role.

KV events (MooncakeStoreKVEvents)

Because this is a shared store, other instances care when blocks are added/evicted. The connector emits KVCacheEvents that a KVEventAggregator collects from all workers, dedups to “common events” (present on all workers), and publishes. That’s what powers external prefix-index consumers.

Cross-layer blocks

Opt-in via enable_cross_layers_blocks. Store handles get one large registered tensor across layers instead of per-layer registrations. Only supported for models without hybrid attention.

Config validation

Explicitly rejects:

  • CrossAttentionSpec (encoder-decoder cross-attn).
  • Mamba layers that aren’t in “align mode” (spec.block_size != cache_config.block_size) — needed because the store keys on logical blocks.
  • Hybrid attention combined with prefill/decode context parallelism > 1.

Load-error reporting

Exposes get_block_ids_with_load_errors so the scheduler can invalidate a bad prefix hit and fall through to local recompute. The P2P connector has no equivalent because a failed transfer aborts the whole request.

Store connector flow

─── Producer side (any instance) ───────────────
Scheduler: update_state_after_alloc → mark blocks to store
Scheduler: build_connector_meta → MooncakeStoreConnectorMetadata

Worker: get_finished(finished_ids, metadata)
└── MooncakeStoreWorker.get_finished(...)
    └── enqueue puts to background thread
        └── store.batch_put(keys=[hash(block)], values=[tensor_slice])
              # Mooncake distributed store handles RDMA internally
        └── emit KVCacheEvent(BlockStored, hash) → aggregator → take_events

─── Consumer side (any instance) ───────────────
Scheduler: get_num_new_matched_tokens
└── MooncakeStoreScheduler probes store for block hashes → returns hit count

Scheduler: build_connector_meta → keys to fetch
Worker: get_finished(...)
└── MooncakeStoreWorker.get_finished(...)
    └── store.batch_get(keys) → writes into registered KV memory
    └── on failure: get_block_ids_with_load_errors() → scheduler recomputes

Key differences vs the P2P flow:

  • No ZMQ side-channel, no bootstrap HTTP — the Mooncake master is the single rendezvous.
  • No _sender_listener / _sender_worker machinery. Both put and get are issued from inside get_finished (start_load_kv is a no-op) so they naturally overlap with compute.
  • No P-D asymmetry: any instance does both puts and gets. Prefix reuse across requests and across instances is automatic because keys are content hashes.

4. Quick comparison

MooncakeConnector (P2P) MooncakeStoreConnector
Transfer model P pushes RDMA writes to D Both put/get against shared store
Discovery Bootstrap HTTP + ZMQ side-channel Mooncake master
Backend call batch_transfer_sync_write MooncakeDistributedStore put/get
Prefix cache reuse Per-request only Fleet-wide via content hash
Best for Single P→D pair, low latency Many-to-many, high prefix hit rate
Hybrid KV support Yes (careful group-preserving logic) Yes, with Mamba align mode required

Both implement SupportsHMA so they interop with hybrid attention KV cache managers, and both go through the scheduler/worker split so the scheduler process only tracks metadata while worker processes own the actual device memory registrations.

item.title: Zero-bubble async scheduling for spec decoding
item.description:
Zhixuan's Blog https://zhixuan-zxli.github.io/llm/async_scheduling/ -

vLLM PR #32951 (refactor of #29957) — how the CPU stops waiting on the GPU when async scheduling meets spec decoding.

Recap: async scheduling without spec decode

  • Scheduler runs one step ahead: while the GPU executes step N, the CPU prepares step N+1.
  • Sampled tokens of step N are not needed to prepare N+1 — the CPU writes -1 placeholders and patches them later.
  • CPU prep of N+1 fully overlaps GPU execution of N → no bubble.

Spec decode breaks this: to prepare step N+1, the CPU must know how many draft tokens were accepted in step N (rejection sampler output), because num_computed_tokens, seq_lens, positions, slot_mapping all depend on it.

The fix: three mechanisms

  1. Optimistic CPU prep — _update_states assumes all drafts accepted; emits -1 placeholders for prev_num_draft_len tokens and a deferred_spec_decode_corrections closure instead of syncing. _prepare_inputs builds optimistic_seq_lens_cpu.
  2. GPU-side correction — update_num_computed_tokens_for_batch_change repairs num_computed_tokens / num_accepted_tokens on the GPU using last step’s valid_sampled_token_count_gpu (never left the device). positions, seq_lens, slot_mapping (_compute_slot_mapping_kernel, triton) are now computed GPU-side from the corrected values.
  3. Deferred CPU correction — after execute_model has launched step N+1’s kernels, the closure runs _get_valid_sampled_token_count() and fixes CPU bookkeeping (req_state.num_computed_tokens, input_batch.num_computed_tokens_cpu). The sync overlaps GPU work.

Timeline

  • vLLM 0.14: bubbles between “target fwd N” & “samp N”, and between “MTP N” & “target fwd N+1”; blocking and redundant D2H copies
  • openPangu 2.0: remove the first buble and the redundant copy
  • vLLM 0.25: remove the blocking D2H from the critical path; GPU correction done by Triton kernel; CPU correction is deferred
